title: Ports, connectors & peripherals
monthTitle: PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)
summary: Learn to recognise the common ports on a PC by their shape, and understand the cables and peripherals that plug into them. This is bread-and-butter knowledge for any helpdesk technician.
objectives: Identify common ports (USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, DisplayPort, RJ45, 3.5mm) by their shape
Explain the difference between USB versions and the speeds they offer
Connect the right peripheral to the right port: keyboard, mouse, monitor, webcam, headset
Describe what a docking station does and when to use one
Recognise legacy ports such as VGA, DVI and PS/2 when you meet older equipment
List connected USB and PnP devices from Windows PowerShell

quiz.q: Which port is small, oval, reversible (works either way up), and can carry power, video and data?
quiz.why: USB-C is the small oval reversible connector. Because it is reversible there is no wrong way up, and a single USB-C port can carry power, video and data at the same time.

quiz.q: A user wants to plug a wired network cable into their laptop. Which port do they need?
quiz.why: RJ45 is the square-ish 8-pin Ethernet port with a little clip. It is wider than a phone jack and is used for wired network connections.

quiz.q: Which of these is a VIDEO connector commonly found on monitors and TVs?
quiz.why: HDMI carries digital video and audio and is the most common modern display connector. RJ45 is networking, PS/2 is legacy keyboard/mouse, and 3.5mm is analogue audio.

quiz.q: Which connector is the older blue D-shaped video port with 15 pins that carries an analogue signal only?
quiz.why: VGA is the legacy blue 15-pin D-shaped port. It carries analogue video only (no audio) and is being replaced by HDMI and DisplayPort.

quiz.q: In one sentence, how can you tell USB-A apart from USB-C just by looking?
quiz.answer: USB-A is the flat rectangular connector that only fits one way up, while USB-C is the small rounded oval connector that is reversible and fits either way.
quiz.why: Shape is the fastest way to identify a port. USB-A is rectangular and one-way; USB-C is oval and reversible.

quiz.q: What is a docking station and why is it useful on a helpdesk?
quiz.answer: A docking station is a hub a laptop connects to (often by a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable) that adds extra ports such as Ethernet, multiple monitors, USB and power, so a user can connect everything with one click.
quiz.why: Docks let a user plug in once and instantly connect monitors, network, keyboard, mouse and power, which is why they are common on office desks and a frequent support topic.

body_markdown:
## Why ports matter on a helpdesk

A huge share of helpdesk tickets are simply "my monitor won't display" or "my mouse stopped working". Nine times out of ten the fix is knowing **which cable goes in which hole**. If you can identify a port by its **shape**, you can solve these in seconds. Let's learn the common ones.

## USB: the universal connector

**USB** (Universal Serial Bus) is the most common port you'll meet. There are two shapes you must know:

- **USB-A** — the flat **rectangular** connector that only fits one way up (everyone flips it three times). Used for keyboards, mice, flash drives.
- **USB-C** — a small **oval, reversible** connector. No wrong way up. It can carry data, video and power all at once.

USB also comes in **versions** that set the speed. **USB 2.0** is slow (often a black plug). **USB 3.x** is faster (often a **blue** plug). **Thunderbolt** uses the USB-C shape but is even faster and can drive monitors and external drives. Tip: blue inside the port usually means it's a faster USB 3 port.

## Video ports: getting a picture on screen

When a monitor shows "No Signal", check the video cable. The common ones:

- **HDMI** — flat with slightly tapered corners; carries **video and audio**. Most common today.
- **DisplayPort** — similar size to HDMI but with one **squared-off** corner; great for high refresh rates.
- **VGA** — old **blue D-shaped** port with 15 pins; **analogue video only**, no sound.
- **DVI** — older white connector with many pins; a step between VGA and HDMI.

## Audio, networking, legacy and power

- **3.5mm jack** — the round headphone/microphone hole. Green is usually output, pink is microphone.
- **RJ45 (Ethernet)** — squarish 8-pin port with a clip, for **wired networking**. Looks like a fat phone socket.
- **PS/2** — round **purple (keyboard)** or **green (mouse)** legacy ports on older desktops.
- **Power** — desktops use a **barrel** plug or a power lead; many modern laptops charge over **USB-C**.

## Peripherals and docking stations

**Peripherals** are the devices users plug in: **keyboard**, **mouse**, **monitor**, **webcam**, **headset**. Most modern ones use USB-A, USB-C or wireless (Bluetooth/USB dongle).

A **docking station** lets a laptop connect to lots of things with **one cable**. The user plugs in a single USB-C or Thunderbolt lead and instantly gets Ethernet, two monitors, USB devices and charging. Docks are common on office desks and a frequent support topic.

## Listing devices in PowerShell

When a USB device misbehaves, you can list what Windows currently sees. Open **PowerShell** and run:

```powershell
Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Where-Object Class -eq 'USB'
```

To see everything Windows detects (not just USB):

```powershell
Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Select-Object Class, FriendlyName, Status
```

If a device shows a Status of `Error`, that's a strong clue where the problem is.

## Your task

Walk over to a PC (or use a photo of one). Identify and write down **at least five ports** by shape: USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, RJ45 and a 3.5mm jack. Then open PowerShell, run `Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Where-Object Class -eq 'USB'`, and note one USB device it lists.

slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Four. Today we're learning the ports and connectors on a computer, and the peripherals that plug into them. This is bread-and-butter helpdesk knowledge. By the end you'll be able to look at the back of any PC and name the ports just by their shape.

slides.title: Why ports matter
bullets: Loads of tickets are "no display" or "mouse dead".
The fix is usually the right cable in the right hole.
Identify a port by its shape and you solve it fast.
slides.narration: Let's start with why this matters. A huge share of helpdesk tickets are simply, my monitor won't display, or my mouse stopped working. Nine times out of ten the fix is knowing which cable goes in which hole. If you can identify a port just by its shape, you can solve these problems in seconds.

slides.title: USB-A and USB-C
bullets: USB-A: flat rectangle, fits one way up only.
USB-C: small oval, reversible, no wrong way.
USB-C carries data, video and power at once.
USB stands for Universal Serial Bus.
slides.narration: The most common port you'll meet is U S B, which stands for Universal Serial Bus. There are two shapes to know. U S B dash A is the flat rectangular plug that only fits one way up. U S B dash C is the small oval connector that is reversible, so there's never a wrong way up, and it can carry data, video and power all at the same time.

slides.title: USB versions & speeds
bullets: USB 2.0 is slow, often a black plug.
USB 3.x is faster, often a blue plug.
Thunderbolt uses USB-C shape but is fastest.
Blue inside a port usually means USB 3.
slides.narration: U S B also comes in versions that set the speed. U S B two point zero is the slow one, often a black plug. U S B three point x is much faster and is often coloured blue. Thunderbolt uses the same U S B dash C shape but is faster still, and can even drive monitors. A quick tip: if the inside of the port is blue, it's usually a faster U S B three port.

slides.title: Video ports
bullets: HDMI: flat, tapered corners, video and audio.
DisplayPort: like HDMI but one squared corner.
VGA: old blue D-shaped 15-pin, video only.
DVI: older white connector, many pins.
slides.narration: When a monitor shows No Signal, check the video cable. H D M I is the common one today and carries both video and audio. DisplayPort looks similar but has one squared-off corner. V G A is the old blue D-shaped port with fifteen pins, and it carries analogue video only, no sound. D V I is an older white connector you'll still meet on some monitors.

slides.title: Audio, network & legacy
bullets: 3.5mm jack: round audio hole, green out, pink mic.
RJ45: squarish 8-pin Ethernet port with a clip.
PS/2: round purple keyboard, green mouse (legacy).
Looks like a fat phone socket? That's RJ45.
slides.narration: A few more to know. The three point five millimetre jack is the round headphone hole; green is usually output and pink is the microphone. R J forty-five is the squarish eight-pin Ethernet port with a little clip, used for wired networking. And on older desktops you'll find P S two, the round purple keyboard and green mouse ports.

slides.title: Power connectors
bullets: Desktops: barrel plug or a mains power lead.
Many modern laptops charge over USB-C.
Wrong charger wattage can charge slowly or not at all.
slides.narration: Power is worth a mention too. Desktops use a barrel plug or a mains lead, while many modern laptops now charge over U S B dash C. Watch out here: if a user plugs in the wrong wattage charger, the laptop may charge very slowly or not at all, which is a common ticket.

slides.title: Peripherals & docking stations
bullets: Peripherals: keyboard, mouse, monitor, webcam, headset.
Most use USB-A, USB-C or wireless.
A dock connects everything with one cable.
One USB-C lead gives Ethernet, monitors, USB, power.
slides.narration: Peripherals are the devices users plug in: keyboard, mouse, monitor, webcam and headset. Most use U S B dash A, U S B dash C, or wireless. A docking station is a clever box that lets a laptop connect to everything with a single cable. The user plugs in one U S B dash C lead and instantly gets Ethernet, two monitors, U S B devices and charging.

slides.title: List devices in PowerShell
bullets: Open PowerShell to see what Windows detects.
Filter to just USB devices, or list everything.
A Status of Error points to the problem.
slides.narration: When a U S B device misbehaves, you can ask Windows what it currently sees. Open PowerShell and run Get dash Pnp Device, dash PresentOnly, piped into Where dash Object Class equals U S B. This lists the connected U S B devices. If any device shows a Status of Error, that's a strong clue about where the problem lies.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Identify ports by shape: USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, RJ45, 3.5mm.
USB 3 is faster than USB 2; Thunderbolt is fastest.
Docks add ports over one cable.
Task: name 5 ports, then list USB devices in PowerShell.
slides.narration: Let's recap. You can now name the common ports by their shape: U S B dash A, U S B dash C, H D M I, R J forty-five and the three point five millimetre jack. Remember U S B three is faster than U S B two, and a dock adds ports over a single cable. Your task: walk to a P C, name at least five ports by shape, then open PowerShell, run Get dash Pnp Device dash PresentOnly filtered to U S B, and note one device it lists. See you in the next lesson.
